newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Gunfire kills two at Pakistan independence rally.
newsitem.headline: Gunfire kills two at Pakistan independence rally.

text.p: At least two people were killed and 20 wounded when a crowd stampeded at a rally for Pakistan's independence day on Thursday, witnesses said.
The violence clouded a day of celebrations to mark the 50 years that have passed since the Indian sub-continent was partitioned at the end of British rule in 1947.
Hospital sources confirmed that two civilian men had died from gunshot wounds.

Witnesses said three other people had been hit in shooting that erupted when police opened fire after shots from the crowd. They said the other casualties were hurt in a police baton charge or were trampled underfoot when people panicked.
The trouble began towards the end of a rally at the mausoleum of Pakistan's founder, Mohammad Ali Jinnah, attended by President Farooq Leghari and Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif.

One official said the mayhem among the estimated 20,000 people at the rally had begun when Sharif motioned for the specatators to come forward. "Security is in the hands of God. Let the people come close," Sharif was quoted as saying.
The crowd then broke through police cordons and rushed towards the podium amid the shrieks of women and children as dozens of people fell and were trampled underfoot.
Leghari had left the scene earlier and Sharif was whisked away when the disturbances worsened.
Police used batons and teargas to disperse the people, who retaliated by hurling stones and shoes, some of which hit Jinnah's huge white marble mausoleum in central Karachi.

Soldiers guarding the mausoleum trained their guns on the crowd, but did not fire, witnesses said. Scouts ran away from the sprawling edifice. Several government officials had to fight their way past hostile crowds after the police baton charge.
Mounted police outside the mausoleum's perimeter wall were pelted with stones.
The clashes in Karachi, where a feud between factions of an ethnic party has killed over 225 people this year, marred the low-key festivities for the Islamic nation's golden jubilee.
In a morning speech at a flag-raising ceremony outside parliament in Islamabad, Sharif called for peace with India and a solution to the bitter 50-year-old Kashmir dispute.

"I hope that India would also respond with the same sincerity by withdrawing its forces from occupied Kashmir and putting an end to atrocities there and hence pave the way for establishment of lasting peace in the region," he declared.
In a speech to the National Assembly (lower house) at one minute past midnight, Sharif praised Kashmiris fighting Indian troops in the two-thirds of Kashmir under New Delhi's control.
"Today mujahideen (guerrillas) are fighting for their independence in occupied Kashmir. God willing, the Kashmiri people will fulfil their mission one day," he said.
"Pakistan will continue to provide moral support to them. Our independence will be complete on the day all our Kashmiri brethren join us in celebrating independence."
Pakistan, which holds one-third of Kashmir, denies Indian charges that it arms, trains and finances the guerrillas, whose insurgency has cost an estimated 20,000 lives since 1990.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since independence, two of them sparked by tension over Kashmir.
